A1.justification: Both PDFs contain readable main texts and appendices describing the same RIZE study. Despite the changed title and organization, the methods, proofs, experiments, and figures can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v2 reports original MuJoCo experiments across five seeds, critic and regularization ablations, and hyperparameter analyses in Section 5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 reports original MuJoCo and Adroit experiments, baseline comparisons, and multiple ablation and sensitivity studies in Section 5 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: The adaptive-target regularizer, distributional critic, objectives, and update procedure in Algorithm 1 are retained. IQN was already documented in v2's appendix; its more explicit identification and the new experimental variants do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: v3 retains the four original MuJoCo locomotion tasks and adds Hopper-v2 and Adroit Hammer-v1. Hammer introduces dexterous manipulation using D4RL demonstrations, substantially broadening the evaluated task domain beyond locomotion.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates IQ-Learn, LSIQ, and SQIL against RIZE. v3 adds Behavior Cloning and CSIL to comparisons on the retained tasks as well as the new tasks, materially strengthening the comparator set. Their citations in v2 did not represent evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 Figure 1 summarizes selected top-25% episodic returns; v3 introduces RLiable aggregate metrics and final-third training averages in Figures 1–2. New Hammer experiments use a 500,000-step horizon and an expert pool selected from the top 100 of 5,000 episodes. Section 4.2 also revises the stated target range from [0,10] to [5,10], although both versions retain initial expert/policy targets of 10/5.

E4.justification: v3 adds empirical reward-bound checks for distributional and point-estimate critics and an HL-Gauss versus MSE experiment in LSIQ. Its regularization study tests shared targets across Walker2d, Ant, and Hammer while retaining the L2 comparison. The earlier expert-only and policy-only TD ablations disappear, and Figure 16b omits the policy-target initialization of 10 and expert-target initialization of 5 shown in v2 Figure 7b.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeds. v3 replaces half-standard-deviation uncertainty bands with 95% confidence intervals and introduces percentile bootstrap intervals stratified over tasks and seeds for aggregate metrics. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds results for Hopper, Hammer, BC, CSIL, aggregate metrics, and new ablations. CSIL becomes a competitive comparator; RIZE's Hammer means exceed several baselines but remain below the expert reference in Figures 2 and 5. Figure 15 shows that a shared target initialized at 10 succeeds on Ant but fails on Hammer. These are new findings and revised summaries, rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains over v2.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the contraction statement from convergence to an optimal distributional value function to convergence to the unique return distribution for the given policy. The substantive reward derivations and appendix proofs remain unchanged; v2 Corollary A.2 and its proof are relocated to v3 Corollary 4.2.

C1.justification: The two central methodological contributions remain adaptive reward targets and distributional critics. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the empirical claims to Adroit/Hammer, including expert-level performance with three demonstrations. The introduction also softens the components being essential to improving training stability.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretation: it attributes CSIL's early advantage to behavior-cloning initialization, explains LSIQ's bounded values through clipping, and discusses how IQN may stabilize rewards within adaptive bounds. Appendix C adds explanations for HL-Gauss failure and for L2 failure under settings tuned for adaptive TD regularization. The existing limitation concerning unproved convergence of alternating SAC updates remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies replay capacity, batch size, 24 quantile levels, 10,000 pretraining steps, and evaluation interval/timing. It also documents Hammer data selection, baseline parameter sweeps, and new task configurations. These materially expand reproducibility information; the existing network descriptions, retained-task settings, and code-access location largely persist.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning through discussions of AILBoost, CSIL, successor-feature matching, and diffusion-based state-only imitation. Appendix C.5 additionally engages work on classification losses and the alternative explanation that distributional-RL gains can arise from loss choice. This substantially broadens the research context while retaining the IQ-Learn/LSIQ lineage.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially rewritten and reorganized: numbered experimental subsections become shorter main-text discussions, detailed critic and regularization analyses move into Appendix C, and the former Appendix B becomes separate implementation and experimental appendices. The title changes, and return-distribution terminology is standardized throughout.

P2.justification: The figures are extensively redesigned: aggregate interval plots replace the original summary display, learning curves are split by demonstration count, and reward-bound overlays and additional ablation panels are introduced. Existing reward/value comparisons move into expanded appendix grids. Table 1 adds tasks and removes columns whose shared settings remain documented in prose.

improvement.justification: Replacing the top-quarter summary with final-third averages and bootstrapped aggregate intervals, adding BC/CSIL comparisons, and documenting essential settings improve empirical credibility and reproducibility. However, the new expert-level Hammer claim overstates the mean returns shown in Figures 2 and 5, and some one-sided and initialization ablations are lost. These tradeoffs support a limited net improvement.
